# Revise an existing paper from locked evidence

Revise `paper.md` using the two locked source records
`evidence_update.md` and `editorial_memo.md`.

The revision must:

- update the Abstract, Results, and Discussion to agree with the current
  design record, primary analysis, sensor-completeness audit, and editorial
  memo;
- use association language appropriate to the study design rather than making
  a causal claim;
- report the current primary group rates, adjusted difference, and confidence
  interval in both the Abstract and Results, and report the current p value in
  Results;
- report the group-specific sensor-dropout rates and explain the stated
  direction of possible bias from the complete-case analysis without
  imputation;
- characterize the ward-level subgroup analysis according to the locked
  records without presenting it as confirmatory;
- bind design statements to `[D1]`, primary-result statements to `[D2]`, and
  missingness or subgroup statements to `[D3]`; and
- add no source, statistic, or recommendation not supported by the locked
  records.

Preserve the title and the complete Introduction, Methods, and References
sections of `paper.md` verbatim. Keep the existing section headings in their
existing order. Do not change `evidence_update.md` or `editorial_memo.md`.
Only `paper.md` should change.

The declared `visible` check covers candidate file identity, locked-source and
protected-section preservation, section structure, obsolete literal markers,
and citation syntax. External grading evaluates the revised evidence claims
and cross-section consistency. Submit when you choose to finish.

Retention was 71.2% with adaptive alerts and 52.8% under usual monitoring (adjusted difference 18.4 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.1 to 30.7) [D1][D2]. The nonrandomized design does not establish causation, and differential sensor dropout could bias the estimated association upward [D1][D3].\n\n## Introduction\n\nLoss of overnight sensor observations can delay recognition of clinical deterioration. Adaptive alerts may improve record retention by identifying interrupted streams before the observation window closes [D1].\n\nWe evaluated whether adaptive alerts were associated with retention of usable overnight sensor records across six inpatient wards.\n\n## Methods\n\nWe conducted a prospective matched-cohort evaluation across six wards. Wards introduced adaptive alerts according to local operational schedules; patients were not randomly assigned. Each intervention observation was matched to a usual-monitoring observation by ward and baseline risk.\n\nThe primary endpoint was retention of a usable overnight sensor record through 06:00. The analysis used complete cases and did not impute missing sensor records. Ward-level subgroup comparisons were exploratory.\n\n## Results\n\nOvernight retention was 71.2% with adaptive alerts and 52.8% with usual monitoring, an adjusted absolute difference of 18.4 percentage points (95% CI, 6.1 to 30.7; p = 0.006) [D2].\n\nSensor dropout affected 8.7% of adaptive-alert observations and 3.1% of usual-monitoring observations. The primary analysis used complete cases without imputation, and the differential dropout could bias the estimated association upward [D3].\n\nWard-level subgroup comparisons were exploratory and were not preregistered; they do not establish effect heterogeneity [D3].\n\n## Discussion\n\nThis matched-cohort evaluation found that adaptive alerts were associated with higher overnight retention, but the nonrandomized design does not establish causation [D1][D2]. Differential sensor dropout could bias the estimated association upward, so the observed difference should be interpreted cautiously [D3]. The ward-level subgroup analysis was exploratory and not preregistered, and it does not provide confirmatory evidence of effect heterogeneity [D3].\n\n## References\n\n[D1] Operations Consortium.
